utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know when you heard that rumour, nor can you remember who told you about such a story; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of any other units that had been billeted in the village at that time? Did you hear any such story or rumours?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from those units and the local residents, there were also a number of refugees which had been accommodated in the village at the time.

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you could see, they had been billeted on both sides of the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, at first. And then later on, only on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But during the time relevant to the matter presently being discussed, refugees had been billeted or were billeted at the time on both sides of the village and you would see them going from one side to the other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they were searching for food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And aside from -- or among those refugees were a number of former camp inmates, people who had been camped in a Croatian camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: First the refugees arrived, and after that the camp inmates arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember, sir, more or less, doing the best with your memory, at what time those camp inmates arrived in the village of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date, but they arrived to Grabovica via Dreznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, sir, I'm not asking for miracles here, but using your memory can you remember whether a group -- a group of camp inmates arrived shortly before the incident in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. They arrived before this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the same day as the day when you were on your shift which you described in your statement? Was it that very day, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: When the camp inmates arrived, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've indicated that refugees would go from one side of the village to the other in search of food. Was it the fact, sir, that at the time everyone in the region but in particular those former camp inmates were desperate for food?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was looking for food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they in particular, sir, some of those refugees obviously had lost a lot of weight during their ordeal in the camps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has read a summary of your statement and has referred to an occasion where, I believe, the commander of Cedo's Wolves came in your office to call Zuka's command. And I just want to ask you a simple question about that incident: Is it the fact, sir, that you only saw Zuka's car coming to the village? You didn't see Zuka himself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, doing the best you can with your memory, sir, but the time at which Zuka's car came in the village, it was still daylight, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution in its summary has also referred to the time when you learnt about killings having taken place in the village. And you learnt about those killings on the morning when you ended your shift; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the day after?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: I took up my shift in the morning, and the incident took place in the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just asking you about when you learnt that civilians had been killed in the village. Was it the morning when you finished your shift, that is, the morning after you heard the shooting in the village? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: No. I heard in the morning when I took up my shift from a Muslim woman called Nena. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember, sir, whether that was that next morning, a day after, two days after? Can you remember that fact? Or is it too far away from your memory. I'm not asking you to -- to make any guess, sir, in that regard. If you don't know, you can simply state so.

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: The first morning after the incident. I came to take up my shift, and that's when I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you've explained that you went to talk to a friend of yours who would go by the first name Andrija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, before this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Andrija was a Croat, was he?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you arrived at his home, instead of Andrija, Muslim refugees answered the door and told you that Andrija had been taken away by the police to protect him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. A Muslim woman called Nena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Nena told you that Andrija had been taken by the police together with other Croat civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that they had been taken for their own protection.

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Nena also told you that those people, including Andrija, had been taken the night before you paid her a visit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: In the morning, I paid Nena a visit at Andrija's house, but this happened during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just so that we're clear about the timing. The incident happened during the night, and the next morning you went to Nena in the hope of seeing Andrija, and that's when she told you that the night before he had been taken away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: That they had been taken in the night. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you had occasion later on when you learned that Andrija had actually been taken to the museum facility in Jablanica to go and visit him; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's also the occasion when you told Andrija that you had seen what you believed to be the dead body of his brother; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions about that particular matter. When you saw the body for the first time, there was no particular mark on the body which would indicate the cause of death; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no entry or exit wound on the body, or none that you could see; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I saw neither an entry nor an exit wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were no bruises on the body.

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't notice any traces of blood in or around the body.

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time, you were unable to determine what he could have died of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: When I saw the body, I said he had been neither killed nor slaughtered. I do not know what the cause of death was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that very conclusion, sir, you mentioned it to the Prosecutor investigator who came to interview you in Jablanica; isn't that correct? You told him, "I don't know what this person died of," and you also told him, "He could have died of natural causes"? Isn't that what you told the prosecuting investigator?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: That was in Sarajevo. That was in Sarajevo when we talked. I said he hadn't been. The investigator said he had. I said he hadn't. And then we agreed that it should be the Court who should decide that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you insisted with the investigator that in your view he could have died about natural causes. And the investigator, if I'm correct, declined or disagreed with you and declined to put that fact in your statement. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we did agree that it should be the Court who should decide that. That was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's very good advice. Can you remember the name of that investigator, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: He was a Russian, but I don't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself by the name Nikolai?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you saw that body again a day or two later. And by that time, the body had been burnt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know who burnt that body, did you -- or do you?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: I don't know who burnt it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw the body on that later occasion after it had been burnt, you saw a large hole - I think you indicated about five centimetres large - at the back of the head of that body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also indicated in 1999 in a statement that you gave to the investigative judge of the cantonal court in Sarajevo that - and I quote - "I can confirm with certainty that this hole on the skull was not there at the time when I first saw the body." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only have very few questions now to ask you about the time after the particular incident. Are you aware, sir, that a colleague of yours from the hydroelectric plant, a man called Osman Kovacevic, was interviewed about the events in Grabovica? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his interview was carried out by the local authorities in Jablanica shortly after the incident; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember whether the person who interviewed him is a man called Ahmed Salihamidzic, who's a member of the civilian police, the MUP, in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Osman didn't talk to me about it, so I don't know. I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any other individuals, whether colleagues from the hydroelectric plant or any other person that you would know of, who were also interviewed shortly after the incident by the local authorities? And you yourself, sir, were you so interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, and there's nothing really I can say about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if your colleague Mr. Alija Turkic was interviewed shortly after this incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The witness has very clearly stated he does not know. And by my learned friend putting to him more and more names, I don't really see the -- the point in that, Your Honour. The witness has very clearly said he doesn't know who was interviewed, and that should be the end of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm just trying to help the memories of -- the memory of the witness in that regard by putting to him a particular name which he could remember or a person which he might have discussed this matter with. This is the only name put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, from the answer of this witness, it is quite clear. He said, "No, I wasn't. There's nothing really I can say about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, that would have been our last question for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour, if I may. Re-examined by Ms. Chana:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neziric, you were asked about where the refugees were, and I would like you to clarify a certain matter in respect of that. First you said they were on both sides and then later on only on the left bank. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we sort of take this incident which happened in Grabovica as a point. Was it before or after? Where were the refugees before this incident and where were the refugees after and during?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object to that. He's answered that question. He's indicated that at the time they were on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but to me it's not still very clear. Maybe we could hear this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: If you look at one point of this case, then the refugees were on both sides until the moment the -- the army from Sarajevo came. When they came, they were only on the left bank of the river. As they were scurrying for food, they were on both banks. However, they were accommodated on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they were scurrying for food, that was after the incident, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the -- I'm sorry, I would object. There should be no leading in re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what he said. I'm just confirming it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think that is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Would you ...

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: The refugees were on both banks, scurrying for food on both sides. Once the troops came, they were only on the left bank because on the other bank there was nothing left. It was over and done with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did the refugees go back scurrying for food?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: When the refugees came from Capljina to Grabovica, they were hungry right away. There was nothing to eat. And they started the process immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in respect with this bank -- this inmates -- camp inmates. When did they arrive? And this is in relation to the incidents. Before or after?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were they housed?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: There was no housing as such. Wherever they landed, they stayed on in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened -- where were these camp inmates once the ABiH, these troops from Sarajevo, came?

utterances.speaker: SABAN NEZIRIC
utterances.text: They were on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That will be all from this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey. You'll say something about the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to say it might be appropriate to take an early break before that witness commences. But my learned friend is here now, so I'm in the hands of the Prosecutor as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Re, are you going to take the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, yes. He's just outside. I just spoke to him. He's -- he's ready to go, if the Trial Chamber is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So could we have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemn declaration that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Eminovic. Some personal details for the record, please, and I will just lead you through some details about yourself. Your name is Nermin Eminovic and you were born on the 12th of October, 1955; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- your present -- or your occupation for some time has been as a clerk in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Federal Ministry of Defence, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did your JNA military service in 1992 -- sorry, 1982 in an engineering unit, and you have qualifications in engineering?.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And using your qualifications in engineering in 1992 when the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were working in a factory in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in April 1992, you joined the Territorial Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And skipping to -- skipping through the next year. In June 1993, upon the formation of the 6th Corps, you took up a position as the assistant to the commander for military -- military security within that corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remained in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina until the beginning of 1996, after the Dayton Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June 1993, when you were the assistant to the commander for military security, were you a member of the military security service?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Let me explain. I was not officially accepted into the military security service. I worked in the military security service. However, I was never officially admitted. This admission, my admission into the service, was done subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior when you worked -- from June 1993 onwards, when you were working in the 6th Corps command?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate commander was the corps commander, Salko Gusic. My immediate superior, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Jusuf Jasarevic? Were you also reporting to him?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about the professional line, as we call it, the official professional line of reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has had -- heard an amount of evidence about the chains of reporting within the military security service, so I don't want to go into any detail with you on that. I just want to clarify that -- in this respect: Are you saying that there was a parallel chain of command and you were reporting to both Salko Gusic and Jusuf Jasarevic because of the duties you had?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so. Salko Gusic was more my immediate commander, and I had to carry out his orders. As for the professional chain, this had to do with my profession, and I did have my obligations towards Mr. Jasarevic, who was the chief of the security administration. I had to inform him about all the important developments that took place in the area of responsibility, in the units and in the commands there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you based at the 6th Corps headquarters in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The corps command in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to briefly tell the Trial Chamber -- if you could list the duties you had in that position.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain. What duties? What tasks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you told the Trial Chamber that you had obligations towards Mr. Jasarevic, who was the chief of the security administration. You had to inform him about all the important developments that took place in the area of responsibility. What I want you to tell the Trial Chamber is: Apart from reporting back to Mr. Jasarevic on those matters, what were your duties, what were your responsibilities, what did you have responsibility for? And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: There was a whole range of duties. My duty was with respect to all important events that had to do with command and control to report them to the commander. It was also my duty to protect the unit in every aspect of command, and my most important job was the counter-intelligence protection of units and persons in the command. Also, one of my tasks was professional leadership of the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Taking them in turn. The first one you mentioned was protecting the unit in every aspect of command. And what did that involve? What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Protection in the broader sense of -- from any kind of sabotage, from discovery. This was a whole set of measures and activities aimed at protecting the unit from the leaking of confidential information. I could say more, but this was it more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just give maybe a brief example of something you did. So that we have a concrete idea of the sort of tasks that you carried out.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: For example, one of the problems was the disappearing of ammunition and weapons from the units. Because of the situation prevailing in Bosnia, there were a lot of people who arrived in our area of responsibility and bought ammunition for money, for tobacco. They would also buy rifles, hand grenades, and other weapons. These were always individuals who did this, and very often organised groups would arrive, and we had to monitor this and provide protection from it in some way. That was one example. Another example, for example, is the construction of the helicopter pad, which was started, and we had to monitor this because we assumed that there could be an enemy attack in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that particular one, yes. Moving to the next one, which was counter-intelligence, can you just briefly give the Trial Chamber an example of what your activities in counter-intelligence in the 6th Corps in the Konjic area involved in 1993.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Konjic and Herzegovina at the time - how shall I put this? - this area was affected by war to a great extent: First the war with the aggressors from Serbia and Montenegro; and later on the betrayal by the HVO. This area was rife with unsolved problems and subordination between the units, communication with the units. All this was prone to numerous problems. And because of previous events, there was a lot of insecurity. Very often they would say to me, "You're some sort of a new command. Commands come and go, but we stay." The biggest problem was to build confidence among the subordinate units and individuals. One of my personal problems within the service was the development and establishment of the service itself. People were there who had been put there without any special criteria or the commander's personal criteria. And in any case, this was not a good thing. The process of building up the service required a lot of time. There had to be selection of personnel. This was new territory for me, so I didn't know the people, and it couldn't be done very quickly. These were some of the problems, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you referred to the service. Were you referring to the military security service?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When -- I am talking about the service. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I may not be precise in my expression. When I say "service," I mean the military security service. I'll try and be very precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that military security service, was that a -- what could be described as a "command service"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain? I don't understand quite understand your "command service" term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't understand it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't understand it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Eminovic, how much contact did you have in your day-to-day tasks with, firstly, Mr. Gusic and, secondly, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I had daily contacts with Mr. Gusic, if he was there and if he needed to see me or I needed to see him. Very often we were on different sides and we didn't see each other for a few days. And as for Mr. Jasarevic, I had contacts with him when he needed to talk to me, when he needed to provide me with some instruction, or when he wanted me to brief him on something. At that time, there were some requests to send daily reports to Mr. Jasarevic. However, given the development of events in the area, it was impossible to meet that request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just talking at the moment generally, in the period from June 1993. Just generally how much contact you had with Mr. Jasarevic and ...

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to my personal contacts or our communication via the communication means?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, both.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As for my personal contacts with him, I may have had four or five such contacts. Not more than that. I may be wrong by two or three. Those were our personal contacts when I went to Sarajevo and when I met with Mr. Jasarevic there. As for our communication via the communication means, if we needed to talk to each other we didn't do it verbally. We communicated via mail or closed lines. And that's how we conveyed documents to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third responsibility you mentioned a little earlier was in relation to the military police. What were your duties and responsibilities with the military police in the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The military police was part of the corps, and the commander was the one who was in command over the military police. My duties vis-a-vis the military police were as follows: In preparation for drafting professional materials that would serve to provide security for certain facilities, I would carry out some corrections. And that was my way of assisting them. Also, when the military police was to be used for some specific tasks, if the need arose, for example, when the court started functioning and when the -- an arrested person had to be escorted to the court, I would assist them with that. This was the scope of my duties vis-a-vis the military police. I did not have a command role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to issue orders at all to the military police?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The commander authorised me in certain cases to issue orders, but only for some very specific tasks. Not for others. For example, we -- when we had to transport a detainee from the prison to the court, I had that authority. I did not have any general authority. Or, for example, if a certain piece of equipment was being requisitioned, then I had the possibility at the request of the Defence Department to send the military police to assist with that task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role, if you -- sorry, what role, if any, did you have in the investigation of criminal offences committed by members of the military?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All information that pointed to that -- let me first tell you that the police was a body that was very often privy to certain information. The police would come back with that information, and then we'd try to investigate. And it was my obligation to discuss all this information with the police, to analyse it, to carry out certain measures that fall under the scope of the police work, and then we would implement these measures. If we decided that a crime had been committed, we would send our criminal report to the court for their procedure. At that time, the military police had all the police authorities, like the civilian police; however, they were limited to the military personnel. We could keep a person in custody for 72 hours if there was a suspicion that this person had committed a crime. If there was evidence that a crime had been committed, the commanders had to sign criminal reports against the perpetrators of those crimes. I'm talking about the unit commanders. And that was a very specific characteristic of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said "to the court." Did you mean investigating judges?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: To be honest --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which court were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, say for the misdemeanour court, when the 6th Corps was established there was no court except for the basic municipal court. There was no military court. There was no other court, for that matter. And on my insistent and as a result of the need that existed, towards the end of August a department of the district military court was established in Konjic. It was not established at the moment. The process began at that time. And sometime in October or maybe a bit sooner, they started functioning in a somewhat more serious way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the crimes were committed in Grabovica, had you personally been involved in any investigations of -- into offences allegedly committed by 6th Corps military personnel?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was information at the time about certain crimes. We embarked on some investigations. We even had some plans at the level of some of the units. The task of all the assistants in the brigades was to gather all the information and to prepare criminal reports. There was information on that sort -- of that sort. Later on in various cases judiciary procedures were initiated. At that time, we were involved in a number of investigations. Primarily in the cases which in a certain way involved contacts with the enemy. I can even specify which cases and which types of acts -- of crimes I have in mind. First of all, there was smuggling, involving the enemy side. This was one of our major problems. There were also a number of crimes that fell under the category of war crimes that had been committed before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly by members of the army, members of the army and of the then-6th Corps. They were in some other units or had been. But as they came under the command of the 6th Corps, there were also members who had committed crimes as members of the army but were no longer members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many military police were in the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: There was a battalion of military police in the 6th Corps, and it had two companies. One company was in Jablanica; the other in Konjic. At the time when the military unit -- the motorised brigade - I think it was called the 302nd Motorised Brigade from Visoko - was part of the corps, it also had a military company but it wasn't there the whole time. We tried to get this company involved in the military police battalion. These two companies, in Jablanica and Konjic, which were there continuously, numbered -- I may be wrong, but about 60 men each. I think that the then-establishment was 76, but the companies were not 100 per cent up to manpower level. Also, there were about 10 men in the battalion command. Approximately 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said one was in Konjic -- Konjic, I'm sorry, and the other in Jablanica. Where was the military police --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in Jablanica were the military police based?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the school there. I don't know how to explain it. There was a school building in which the command of the 44th was also located and some sort of battalion. There was a military unit there, and the investigations department of that company was located in a building in the town. I don't know the exact address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the geographical distance between Konjic and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is it the right time for us to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could just ask one more question on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the -- how long in September 1993 would it take -- would it have taken you to travel between Konjic and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a vehicle, about six hours, let's say. Roughly speaking. I think it would have taken four, five, six, or seven hours, depending on your vehicle. On foot, you could reach it in four or five hours. The reason for this is that you had to take a forest road which was a roundabout road, and the asphalt road was interrupted in Dretelj - that was the HVO state - about 400 or 500 metres, or maybe a kilometre at the most. This was not passable. That's how it was in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 6th Corps military police in August and September 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Nusret Sahic. That was his name, his first and last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, who was he in August and September 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: General Halilovic held the post of Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever visit the 6th Corps headquarters in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I personally know that General Halilovic visited the command of the 6th Corps on one occasion. I think this was in late August. I cannot be sure about this, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do when he came to the 6th Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: General Halilovic, I think, had a visit of some kind which was not announced. It was in passing. I couldn't really explain. He just happened to be there. I probably wouldn't even remember this visit had it not been for a recollection I have. There were several brigade commanders there and Mitko Pitkic, the commander of the 43rd Brigade was present. What sticks in my memory, and to be quite honest, I don't even know why I was there. Perhaps as host. I'm not sure. But he was a bit rough with the commander of the 43rd Brigade. In my view, this was unjustified. And that's the reason why I recall that visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember now whether Mr. Gusic, the commander, was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure. I am really not sure. The reason I remember it was that General Halilovic was quite rough with the commander of the 43rd Brigade and the man wept. That's why I remember it. I don't know who else was there. This is the only detail I can recall. There was nothing else that sticks in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about what the meeting was about? Can you remember what the meeting was about?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was a military meeting in the sense of being a briefing, a debriefing, an issuing of tasks, or anything like that. It was more talk about politics and the usual kind of things people talk about. It was just a visit in passing. He dropped in. That's how I experienced it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what a forward command post is?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any forward command posts in the area in which you were working in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: According to what there was in the written documents and what people said, there was a forward command post in Donja Jablanica of the Supreme Command. That's what I can say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find out about this forward command post in Donja Jablanica of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know much. I only know that the Chief of Staff was there, General Halilovic, and that with him in his team were Mr. -- or rather, later Brigadier Vehbija Karic, General Suljevic, I think General Bilajac, and there was Namik Dzankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of this forward command post? Or who was in command of the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's been clear evidence from military experts here that no one is in command of a military command post. It's a command post. There's a question here that can be asked which I don't object to, and that's who was in command of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. It's a fair point. I'll proceed that way just to save time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, you said there was a team. What was the team called?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know what the team was called. To be quite honest, later on I found out what its name was. At that moment, I didn't know. At that moment for me this was just a forward command post. I am referring to the time of August and September 1993. That's the time period I'm referring to. I learned other details later on, and perhaps this can prompt me to say things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What did you learn that this team was called later?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was an inspection team or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the senior commander of this forward command post in Donja Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the objection I made before. And it's -- my objection really is to the use of the term "commander" in juxtaposition to the "forward command post." I don't object to this witness giving his -- his evidence as to who was the senior out of those people or anything of that nature. That's not my objection. So just so my friend understands what I'm objecting to. It's that "commander" plus "command post" juxtaposition that's concerning me, given the evidence that's already been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since there's a forward command post, there must be somebody or a group of people in charge of that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour, it's a military doctrinal problem that this court -- this Tribunal might have to deal with at a future time, because the evidence that we've sought to elicit in -- in evidence - and I think the record shows that we have with Mr. Cikotic and others - is that a forward command post as such doesn't of itself have a commander. It's a command post. It's a place. And that the question of a commander as -- as being the commander of a unit or of a team or of some other collection of individuals. So that's the basis of the objection. And it's a question of characterising at a later time -- I mean, bearing in mind many of the questions -- I don't want to make a speech about, this Your Honour. I'm just aware of not doing so. It's that juxtaposition that concerns me. It's not the question of who was the senior in this witness's perception. Of course he can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. Yes, Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was directed at who was the senior commander at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The senior officer was the Chief of Staff, General Halilovic. There was no higher military authority at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in command of the team at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't understand this question: Who was in command of the team? What team are you referring to? Can you clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The forward command post, what was your understanding of who -- I withdraw that. You said General Halilovic was the senior officer at the forward command post. Who was in charge or, sorry, in command of those stationed at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I was not involved in any work. To me, these are just people who have come from the superior command. But I was not involved in their work. I wasn't present. So I don't know how all this functioned. I do know that General Halilovic was the greatest military authority there. That was my understanding. If I may be of assistance in any other way, I will be happy to be, but that was my understanding of matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Where in Donja Jablanica was this forward command post?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: As I just said, I wasn't there at the time, but later on I learnt precisely where it had been because I passed by that place. How can I explain it? That was where Zuka's base was, as far as I could understand, and it was right next to it. This was a cluster of houses. When we speak of a base or a command post, this was not fenced off. These were residential buildings where a forward command post or a staff or some other sort of post could be set up, and this was in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Zuka, that's Zulfikar Alispago?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was his unit subordinated to, in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a detachment for special purposes of the Supreme Command Staff Zulfikar. I think this was its name: The special purpose detachment of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar where -- with where the village of Grabovica is?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say now whether it was within the 6th Corps area of responsibility as of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was, but the best answer would be to consult an operations officer. He would be the one who would be best equipped to provide an answer for this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about your memory now, as opposed to September 1993. In September 1993, would you have known whether it was within the area of responsibility of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Probably, yes. Because at that time, in September 1993, I could have found it out very easily. I could have asked someone and I would have known about it very quickly if I needed to know. The reason I'm saying this is that according to the organisation order on the establishment of the 6th Corps, it was done according to municipality. In September 1993, I didn't even know that Grabovica belonged to the Mostar municipality, so it was municipalities that were mentioned in the order. The Mostar municipality, according to the organisation order, did not belong to the 6th Corps. Probably this was regulated in subsequent orders. But the operations officers would definitely have been familiar with it, so it would be best to consult them. This was not my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of an operation called Neretva?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: An operation called Neretva. I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When? I just want the approximate date and then I'll move on to another question. So if you could please give me a very brief answer to that one.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: It was approximately around the time of these events. But to be quite honest, I did not participate in any kind of planning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want you to very -- I just -- if you could please assist me in this way and please listen very carefully to the question. My question was only as to when you found out. And I'll just move to another one afterwards. So thank you for that. You said it was around the time of the events. Which events are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the events in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it was before or after the events in Grabovica that you heard about -- heard out -- sorry, heard about an operation called "Neretva"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The name of the operation is something I probably heard later on, but I did have knowledge that something was being done and planned. I had certain information based on movements of the army and so on, that something was afoot, but nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which movements of the army are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, there were movements in that troops arrived from Sarajevo. I am referring to members of units from Sarajevo. That was the information I had at the time. I didn't know what the units were or why they were arriving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you obtain your information that these troops were arriving from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Based on police reports - I'm referring to the military police - they were the ones controlling the territory, and I knew that there were movements and that troops were arriving from Sarajevo. Units from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they staying?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, most of them were billeted in Jablanica and lower down in Grabovica. At least, that's what transpired later. When I say "Jablanica," I'm referring to Jablanica municipality. I didn't know that they were billeted in other places possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time, when the troops were being billeted in -- the soldiers from Sarajevo were being billeted in Jablanica municipality, of whether or not there were any military police with those troops?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know under whose command the soldiers from Sarajevo were? That is, who brought them there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question -- that's two questions there, and they mean different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could ask it one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first question, Mr. Eminovic: Do you know under whose command the soldiers from Sarajevo were?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who brought them to the area, the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, no. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Dzankovic's role, to your knowledge, in the inspection team at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Dzankovic, I think, in late August. That was my first meeting with him. That's when we got to know each other. I knew that he was coming from the superior house. I think -- I know that he was a member of the team and that he was in charge of business of the military security service. He was from the military security service administration. And we agreed that he should carry out his job in the way he thought best and that I would assist him wherever I could and provide whatever support he needed. I would assist him to the extent that I was able to. I am referring only to tasks falling within the compass of the military security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript reads that you said, "I knew that he was coming from the superior house." Did you say "house," or did you use some other term? That's what our translation says.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did use the term "superior house." I was referring to my superior command. He was coming from the Supreme Command Staff or, rather, from the security service administration of the Supreme Command Staff. Sometimes I use imprecise terms. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's -- there's no need to apologise, Mr. Eminovic. What I want to ask you now is where you met Mr. Dzankovic for the first time in, I think you said, late August 1993.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, it was in late August. I think he came to see me at the corps command. We met there two or three times in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first hear about anything happening at Grabovica? And how -- and how did you hear?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 10th of September, 1993. I received information from the battalion commander of the military police, who was then stationed in Jablanica. This information reached me by telephone. At that time, we had several telephone lines at our disposal. As this was an open line, communication could not be open. It was quite closed. What he told me - I will try to paraphrase it now - was that something ugly had happened down there, words to that effect, and that was the information that reached me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand he meant by "something ugly had happened down there"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "ugly," he may have said there were victims or that there had been murders. I am paraphrasing what I heard. It was words to that effect, but I couldn't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you understand "down there" to mean?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: "Down there" in my language -- well, when you're using a telephone line that someone can listen in to - and we used it only when we had to, not usually - and as I knew that he was in Jablanica, if he said to me that it was further south or, rather, "down there," then I would know it was in that area. But at the time, I didn't have anything more precise. This was only preliminary information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your response, Mr. Eminovic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: In that conversation, I suggested to him that he should go and see for himself, that he should go and check, that he should go to the spot and report to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Dzankovic involved at that -- at that point?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I suggested to him that he should communicate with Mr. Dzankovic without fail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this -- who was the battalion commander of the military police who told you this information? Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Nusret Sahic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier about your subordination to Mr. Gusic, on the one hand, in the 6th Corps and Mr. Jasarevic of the security service on the other. As a result of this information, did you have any contact with either Mr. Gusic or Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I communicated with Mr. Jasarevic but also with Mr. Gusic, the commander. I can't recall now the precise time and manner, but in any case, it was my duty, my obligation, to inform both of them about the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D224.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, MFI D224.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It should come up on the screen just in front of you, Mr. Eminovic. Now, that's a document signed by Mr. Jasarevic dated the 12th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's in B/C/S. Could we have the English version. Yes, now we have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the Bosnian original in front of you, Mr. Eminovic, still?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a document that you received in the course of your work in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably through cryptographic protection communication. There was no other way of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who was it addressed to? It says: "6th Corps command to chief of the military security service." Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: This is addressed to me directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember now - this is in 2005 - whether you had communication with Mr. Jasarevic before, whether telephone, radio, or written, before he sent you this -- this order on the 12th of September?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Before what? I did communicate, but about what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the -- the contents of the order, that is: "We are in possession of unverified information that the unit commanded by Ramiz Delalic, aka Celo, has massacred civilians in some Croatian village in the zone of responsibility of the 6th Corps." What I'm asking you was: Had you had any communication with Mr. Jasarevic about Grabovica before you received this order from him?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think that there was any communication about Grabovica or these problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your response to this order? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 13th of October that I received from the commander of the military police battalion a report on his visit to Grabovica and his information about this event, and I forwarded this immediately to the chief of the administration, Mr. Jasarevic, and then proceeding to work on this, I attempted to respond to the tasks assigned me in this document by Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you about the task in one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, could Exhibit P119 please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's coming Mr. Eminovic, what were -- what was -- you said you attempted to respond to the task. What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I sent the commander of the military police battalion toward the scene of the crime and told him to communicate to Namik Dzankovic, who had more firsthand information, who had information better than mine, and to get from him a reply as to what all this was really about. After this, I tried to obtain information that might shed light on these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you referred to receiving a report from the commander of the military police battalion. The transcript says the 13th of October. Did you say October or September?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of September. It couldn't be October. I may have made a slip. I don't know. But I was thinking of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's an easy mistake to make. If you'd just look at the document - can you now see it in front of you on the screen - which is dated the 13th of September, 1993 and signed by Mr. Nusret Sahic addressed to your attention. Was that the document that you were referring to a moment ago; namely, the report from the commander of the military police battalion?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other communications with Mr. Sahic about what he should do when you received this document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: After this, I communicated with him orally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to make one thing clear: Did you tell him to go to the scene of the crime after receiving this report from him or before receiving the report from him?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Before. Before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of receiving this report from him, did you give him further tasks? And if so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. To try to get as much information as possible about the perpetrators and the victims. You can see from his report here that there was communication with Mr. Dzankovic, that he said that the forward command post of the Supreme Command Staff is aware of everything, and that the orders were that nothing should be done because of the planned action. This referred to arrests and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Which was the planned action? The English translation says "planned operation." That -- that's -- that doesn't particularly matter. But for the purposes of your understanding, what -- what was the planned operation?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in our part of the world, we often use the word "action" to describe smaller military operations. Maybe this is why the discrepancy arose. This was the military activity that had been planned and that was beginning. That's what the reference was to. I don't know what else it could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which military activity was that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: This was Operation Neretva 93. That's what it was called officially. At that point, I didn't know that was its name, but this is what I know about the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your professional opinion, having received this document that said that the Supreme Command Staff forward command post had ordered that no arrests be made because there was a forthcoming operation?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: My professional opinion was that this instruction was to be obeyed, and what could I do about it? That was one reason, and there were other reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the other reasons?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: The other reasons were that these were units which were not part of the 6th Corps and were not under the command of the 6th Corps. The third reason was that there was nothing to be relied on officially. I'm not speaking here of command and control. "Command" is something else. But I had no one there I could communicate with within the service and get new information from. One of the reasons at the time was that any police operation not properly supported and well-planned would probably not be successful and there would have been bloodshed. At the time, there were insufficient forces and because -- in view of the military operation, there was not the inclination either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, having received a -- an order from General Jasarevic saying that he was in possession of unverified information that Celo's unit had massacred civilians in a Croatian village and then having received a report from the commander of the military police battalion saying that the Supreme Command Staff forward command post had ordered -- or it had ordered that nothing be done, that is, no arrests be made because there was a forthcoming operation, what was your professional view of the juxtaposition of those two things, a report of a massacre and an order not to arrest anyone? Apart from the fact that you said that you had to obey that order, what was your view as a professional within the military security service or -- or as the assistant commander for military security?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what professional opinion you're referring to, but I don't know -- can you clarify what you mean by "professional opinion"? In what sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the response of that document - that's Mr. Jasarevic document - of the IKM according to the document, one which you'd expect in accordance with the rules, the military security rules, the disciplinary rules, and the criminal laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, it's very difficult to answer this question. There is a possibility the command can probably postpone some activities until later because carrying out these activities would cause greater damage. So certain activities could be postponed until later. That is a risk taken by the command. That's my professional opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you respond to Mr. Jasarevic's order?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can the witness please be shown Exhibit P214, which I note for the record appears to be identical to MFI D234 except that they've -- one's been translated by the Prosecution and the other by the Defence, but it's the same source document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, how about the previous document, that is, P199 [sic]? Is that admitted into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It has a P number. I'm assured that it has been. If it's an MFI number, it hasn't been. P119.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: My recollection is that that was admitted. I'm sorry, we don't have a proper number now. I believe that was admitted when Mr. Gusic gave his evidence quite some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The only query I have about it is that it's a -- it's a document that appears on its own, I think in the 65 ter list, and also as an annexure to another document, and it may be that it's annexed to the document that's about to appear now. That's the only doubt I have. But I think Mr. Cengic is looking now to see whether we can see where it is in the exhibit list. Oh, I think it is in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, 00199. I have it here on my list but I have no documents attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's P119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, anyway, you may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document I want to show the witness is P214. His Honour was asking about P119.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The document to which Your Honour referred earlier is admitted into evidence at P119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, do you have the document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my document, the one that I sent to General Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the information in it accurate to the best of your knowledge then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is accurate. At that time, this is the information that we had at our disposal. And to be honest, nobody at the time had a whole picture. This was just one piece of information that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Jasarevic's response to your sending that report to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can MFI D225 please be brought up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the next document is coming, Mr. Eminovic, what was Mr. Jasarevic's response to your sending that information to him?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that up to this report and up to this incident there was no intense communication and all of a sudden there was an avalanche of requests at the time. On the 15th, Mr. Jasarevic sent me a list of tasks and his request for reports to be sent. This request was sent through the command of the 6th Corps; although, this paper that I have in front of me makes a reference to Mr. Dzankovic. At that time, this was a somewhat peculiar way of communicating. However, my service was used to send a letter to another person, but this document was also sent to me, and you can see here that a joint task was given to me and to Dzankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what was your response to receiving this document or this order from Mr. Jasarevic, which is dated the 15th of September?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to collect some information, as much as I could at the time, because I knew that Namik Dzankovic -- I was sure of that because he was a member of the service, that he also communicated with General Jasarevic at the same time as me. I tried to elucidate as much as possible the whole situation from my position, from the position of the chief of administration, and the chief of corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said you tried to collect some information, as much as you could. What did you do to try and collect the information?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: There are my requests to the assistant commander of the 44th Brigade whose name was Zajko Sihilic, I believe. I asked him to collect information and to meet with Namik Dzankovic and assist him as well. Also, the military police battalion had a task to obtain information and refer the information to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Can the witness please be shown the next document, which is MFI D226, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while that's coming, Mr. Eminovic: As a result of having this information collected, did you in fact report back to Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. This is a short report on the events. It is an attempt to summarise all the information that was collected up to then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the information contained in this document, which is MFI D226, the -- your report to Mr. Jasarevic of the 17th of September, 1993, was that based upon all the sources and information that you had asked to be collected over the previous few days?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. This is a summary of all the information. And to be honest, at the time everything pointed to two possible sources. One was the police station, and the other possible source of information was the situation on the ground. There was not much information from the ground because there was no communication. I believe that most of the information came from the police sources. And when I say "the police sources," I imply the police station, the civilian police station in Jablanica, because the cooperation between the military police and the civilian police was correct and at a rather professional level. Their chains of command were separate, and so were the lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the document, there's an underlined sentence towards the bottom that says: "The entire IKM of the SVK in Jablanica has been briefed about this event."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's on the second page in the English translation. If that could be shown to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the IKM in Jablanica briefed about the event?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they were informed. I believe that they knew what this was all about. I personally don't know how they were informed. Here I see the addressee as being the Supreme Command Staff of the IKM. Maybe you can tell how they were informed if you look at the body of this document. Edib Saric -- Could you please hold on just for a moment. I would like to look at the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Take -- take your time.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that only Zuka could enter this area without any consequences. It says that he issued a report on the events, the contents of which we are not aware of, and this report was forwarded to the command in Sarajevo, according to our operative information, and so on and so forth. It is possible that a reference is being made to Zulfikar Alispago, who made a report. I believe that members of the team at the IKM did -- I don't know where this came from. I believe that there was information based on which this was drafted, because this is some sort of a -- a summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you're saying that you could not longer remember where it came from?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that most of the information came from the police sources. And when I say "the police sources," I imply first and foremost the police station or the public security station, as it was known at the time. Its head was Mr. Zebic. In other words, the information came from the operatives on duty, the policemen who cooperated with the military police company. They had very close cooperation. And I believe that the majority of information came from that -- that direction. In those units, I did not have any official body or organ or person with whom I could communicate. I am implying to the units who came from Sarajevo and who participated supposedly in these crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just under that sentence I was asking you to comment on - that's on page 2 of the English - it says: "For the time being, it is impossible to conduct on-site investigations because of the large number of units, the mood of the units under Ramiz Delalic's command, and the fear that given prominence to this event would result in revolt and the return of all units to Sarajevo which Ramiz Delalic clearly hinted at in talks about this event at Zuka's flat." I just want to ask you to comment on that. What was, if you can now remember, the source of your information for that particular line which you've put in what you called "a summary report"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN EMINOVIC
utterances.text: I find it very difficult. As I say, this report is a summary based on several pieces of information. I really couldn't tell you who the source of this particular information was. Why did I write this down? This was some sort of an assessment of the situation in the unit that was headed by Ramiz Delalic. It described the situation and the mood in that unit, and that hence this sentence.
